sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Micropiles are used for (1) structural support (new foundations, underpinning, seismic retrofitting, support of earth retaining structures) and (2) in-situ reinforcement (slope stabilization and earth retention, ground strengthening, settlement reduction, structural stability) (Figure 3-1). Table 3-1 relates each application to design behavior (CASE 1 or 2) and construction type: structural support is CASE 1, probably 95 percent of world applications.
sections.body: (p. 3-1) Micropiles are currently used in two general application areas: (1) structural support and (2) in-situ reinforcement (Figure 3-1). Structural support includes new foundations, underpinning of existing foundations, seismic retrofitting and foundation support for earth retaining structures. In-situ reinforcement is used for slope stabilization and earth retention, ground strengthening, settlement reduction and structural stability. Table 3-1 summarizes the typical design behavior and micropile construction type for each application. The chapter describes the factors influencing the choice of micropiles and example applications for structural support and in-situ reinforcement on transportation and other civil engineering projects.
key_points: Two application areas: structural support and in-situ reinforcement (Figure 3-1)
Structural support: new foundations, underpinning, seismic retrofitting, support of earth retaining structures
In-situ reinforcement: slope stabilization and earth retention, ground strengthening, settlement reduction, structural stability
Table 3-1: structural support is CASE 1, Type A (bond in rock or stiff clays) or Types B, C, D in soil, probably 95 percent of world applications
Table 3-1: in-situ reinforcement is CASE 1 and/or CASE 2 with Types A and B in soil, 0 to 5 percent of use
figures: Figure 3-1: Classification of Micropile Applications (structural support: foundations for new structures, underpinning of existing foundations, seismic retrofitting, earth retaining structure foundations, with repair or replacement, upgrading of capacity, arresting or prevention of movement and scour protection; in-situ reinforcement: slope stabilization and earth retention, ground strengthening, settlement reduction, structural stability) (p. 3-2)
tables: Table 3-1: Relationship Between Micropile Application, Design Behavior and Construction Type (modified after FHWA, 1997): structural support (underpinning of existing foundations, new foundations and seismic retrofitting), CASE 1, Type A (bond zones in rock or stiff clays) and Types B, C and D in soil, probably 95 percent of total world applications; in-situ earth reinforcement, together 0 to 5 percent: slope stabilization and earth retention, CASE 1 and CASE 2, Types A and B in soil; ground strengthening, CASE 2 with minor CASE 1, Types A and B in soil; settlement reduction, CASE 2, Type A in soil; structural stability, CASE 2, Type A in soil (p. 3-3)
sections.applicability: Overview of micropile application areas and how application relates to design behavior and grouting type.

sections.title: Feasibility of Micropiles
sections.summary: Feasibility of micropiles is treated under 3.2.1 Overview through 3.2.7 Economics of Micropiles; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 3-1) No text is printed under this heading; see 3.2.1 Overview, 3.2.2 Physical Considerations, 3.2.3 Subsurface Conditions, 3.2.4 Environmental Conditions, 3.2.5 Existing Structure Adaptation, 3.2.6 Micropile Limitations and 3.2.7 Economics of Micropiles.
key_points: Feasibility: physical, subsurface and environmental conditions, existing structure adaptation, limitations, economics (3.2.1-3.2.7)
sections.applicability: Pointer to the feasibility factors for micropiles (3.2.1 to 3.2.7).

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Micropiles may be feasible where the project has restricted access or is remote, support must be close to existing structures, ground and drilling are difficult (karst, uncontrolled fills, boulders), pile driving would cause liquefaction, vibration or noise must be minimized, hazardous or contaminated spoil would be generated, or the support must be adapted to an existing structure.
sections.body: (pp. 3-1 to 3-3) Micropiles have specific advantages compared with more conventional support systems. In general they may be feasible under the following project-specific constraints: the project has restricted access or is located in a remote area; the support system needs to be in close pile proximity to existing structures; ground and drilling conditions are difficult (e.g., karstic areas, uncontrolled fills, boulders); pile driving would result in soil liquefaction; vibration or noise needs to be minimized; hazardous or contaminated spoil material will be generated during construction; and adaptation of the support system to an existing structure is required. Limitations and cost information are also presented in this section.
key_points: Restricted access or remote site
Support needed close to existing structures
Difficult ground and drilling (karst, uncontrolled fills, boulders)
Pile driving would cause soil liquefaction
Vibration or noise must be minimized
Hazardous or contaminated spoil would be generated
Support system must be adapted to an existing structure
sections.applicability: Project constraints under which micropiles may be feasible compared with conventional support.

sections.title: Physical Considerations
sections.summary: Micropile drilling and grouting equipment is relatively small and can work in restrictive areas, low headroom (Figure 3-2), close to existing walls or foundations (with space for the drill head and a safe work zone, or by battering), under overhead power lines, up steep slopes and in remote locations; proper drilling and grouting procedures do not damage adjacent structures or ground.
sections.body: (p. 3-3) The drilling and grouting equipment used for micropile installation is relatively small and can be mobilized in restrictive areas that would prohibit conventional pile installation equipment; Figure 3-2 shows micropiles installed in low headroom. Micropiles can be installed in close proximity to existing walls or foundations, provided there is space above for the drill head and a safe work zone or the micropiles are battered to provide this space. Installation is not as affected by overhead power lines or other obstructions as conventional piling, and the equipment can be mobilized up steep slopes and in remote locations. Drilling and grouting for micropiles do not damage adjacent existing structures or affect adjacent ground conditions when proper drilling and grouting procedures are used.
key_points: Small equipment works in restrictive areas and low headroom (Figure 3-2)
Can be installed close to existing walls or foundations if there is space for the drill head, or by battering
Less affected by overhead power lines; equipment can reach steep slopes and remote sites
Proper drilling and grouting procedures do not damage adjacent structures or ground
sections.applicability: Access, headroom and proximity advantages of micropile equipment.

sections.title: Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Micropiles can be installed in difficult, variable or unpredictable ground: cobbles and boulders, fills with buried utilities and debris, irregular lenses of competent and weak materials. Soft clays, running sands and high groundwater that hinder drilled shafts have minimal impact, and micropiles are commonly used in karstic limestone.
sections.body: (p. 3-4) Micropiles can be installed in areas of particularly difficult, variable or unpredictable geologic conditions, such as ground with cobbles and boulders, fills with buried utilities and miscellaneous debris, and irregular lenses of competent and weak materials. Soft clays, running sands and high groundwater not conducive to conventional drilled shafts cause minimal impacts to micropile installation. Micropiles are commonly used in karstic limestone formations.
key_points: Suited to cobbles and boulders, fills with buried utilities and debris, irregular lenses of competent and weak materials
Soft clays, running sands and high groundwater have minimal impact (unlike drilled shafts)
Commonly used in karstic limestone formations
sections.applicability: Ground conditions in which micropiles can be installed where other systems struggle.

sections.title: Environmental Conditions
sections.summary: Micropiles suit hazardous and contaminated soils (little spoil; flush effluent contained). Grout can resist aggressive groundwater: a secant micropile screen with anti-acid mortar protected a Barcelona diaphragm wall from groundwater with pH as low as 1.7 (Bachy, 1992; Figure 3-3). Light equipment suits sensitive, swampy or soft areas; less noise and vibration than driven piles; installation need not open a conduit through a contaminated aquifer.
sections.body: (pp. 3-4 to 3-6) Micropiles can be installed in hazardous and contaminated soils: their small diameter produces less spoil than conventional drilled piles, and flush effluent can be controlled at the surface by containerization or lined pits, greatly reducing the potential for surface contamination and handling costs. Grout mixes can be designed to withstand chemically aggressive groundwater and soils, with special admixtures against acidic and corrosive environments. For example, a micropile 'screen' of overlapping (secant) micropiles was built beside the existing concrete diaphragm wall of an underground parking garage in Barcelona, Spain (Bachy, 1992), which was deteriorating from extremely aggressive groundwater (chlorides and sulfates, pH as low as 1.7) from an adjacent metallurgical plant (Figure 3-3); no trace of acid was detected in samples of the wall collected after the screen was built. Micropiles can be installed in environmentally sensitive areas, including fragile natural settings; the equipment is smaller and lighter than pile driving or shaft drilling equipment and can work in swampy or soft surface soils with minimal impact, and portable equipment is frequently used where access is restricted. Micropiles cause less noise and vibration than conventional piling, especially driven piles, whose vibration can be transferred through the soil to adjacent structures, so they can protect sensitive structures and equipment in old urban and industrial areas. Where a contaminated aquifer overlies the bearing strata, micropiles can be installed in a manner preventing contamination of lower aquifers, unlike driven piles that may form a vertical conduit for contaminant migration.
key_points: Suitable in hazardous and contaminated soils: less spoil; flush effluent contained in containers or lined pits
Grout mixes and admixtures can resist chemically aggressive groundwater and soils
Barcelona example: secant micropile screen with anti-acid mortar protected a diaphragm wall from groundwater with pH as low as 1.7 (Bachy, 1992)
Lighter equipment suits environmentally sensitive, swampy or soft-surface areas
Less noise and vibration than conventional piling, especially driven piles
Can be installed without creating a conduit from a contaminated aquifer to lower aquifers
figures: Figure 3-3: Protection of an Existing Diaphragm Wall with a Secant Micropile Screen using Anti-acid Mortar (after Bachy, 1992) (p. 3-5)
sections.applicability: Micropiles in contaminated, aggressive or sensitive environments and where noise, vibration or aquifer protection matter.

sections.title: Existing Structure Adaptation
sections.summary: Micropiles can be added to an existing pile cap, avoiding a larger footing, to resist added compression, tension and moment, where utilities or structures prevent enlarging the cap; the analysis must consider the relative stiffness of the micropiles and existing piles to estimate individual loads.
sections.body: (p. 3-6) Micropiles can be added to an existing pile cap, eliminating the need for an increased footing size, and effectively resist the additional compression, tension and moment from increased structural loads. Adjacent utilities and/or structures often prevent enlarging existing pile caps, eliminating more traditional piling systems. Design analyses then need to consider the relative stiffness of the micropiles and the existing piles to estimate individual loads.
key_points: Micropiles can be added to an existing pile cap instead of enlarging the footing
They resist added compression, tension and moment from increased structural loads
Analyses must consider relative stiffness of micropiles and existing piles to estimate individual loads
sections.applicability: Adding micropiles to existing pile caps instead of enlarging footings.

sections.title: Micropile Limitations
sections.summary: Vertical micropiles may be limited in lateral capacity and cost effectiveness; inclined installation significantly enhances lateral capacity. Their high slenderness ratio may make them unacceptable for conventional seismic retrofitting where liquefaction may occur (buckling from loss of lateral support). Slope stabilization use is increasing, but performance data should be collected while design procedures evolve.
sections.body: (p. 3-6) Vertical micropiles may be limited in lateral capacity and cost effectiveness; the ability to install them on an incline, however, significantly enhances their lateral capacity. Because of their high slenderness ratio (length/diameter), micropiles may not be acceptable for conventional seismic retrofitting in areas where liquefaction may occur, because of concerns of buckling from loss of lateral support. The use of micropiles for slope stabilization continues to increase, but performance data should be collected on such projects as experience and detailed design procedures continue to evolve.
key_points: Vertical micropiles may be limited in lateral capacity and cost effectiveness; inclined micropiles significantly enhance lateral capacity
High slenderness ratio: may be unacceptable for seismic retrofit where liquefaction may occur (buckling from loss of lateral support)
Collect performance data on slope stabilization projects while design procedures evolve
sections.applicability: Lateral capacity, buckling and slope stabilization limitations of micropiles.

sections.title: Economics of Micropiles
sections.summary: The lineal cost of micropiles usually exceeds that of conventional piling, especially driven piles (costs in Chapter 10). Micropiles are unlikely to compete on an open site with soft, clean, uniform soils and unrestricted access, but can be most cost-effective for delicate underpinning of a bridge pier in a busy old area. Compare total project cost, e.g., $/kN of axial capacity, including right-of-way, utilities, excavation and shoring, footings, hazardous materials, dewatering, erosion control, access, ground improvement and disruption.
sections.body: (pp. 3-6 to 3-7) The lineal cost of micropiles usually exceeds that of conventional piling systems, especially driven piles; costs are discussed in Chapter 10. Cost effectiveness depends on many factors and should be assessed from the physical, environmental and subsurface factors above: for an open site with soft, clean, uniform soils and unrestricted access micropiles will likely not be competitive, but for the delicate underpinning of an existing bridge pier in a heavily trafficked old industrial or residential area they can be the most cost-effective solution. The true final cost of a micropile solution should be defined from all related costs for the entire project, not just the unit cost of the piling; as with other piles it helps to compare micropile costs in $/kN of axial capacity when evaluating deep foundation alternatives. Related costs include right-of-way acquisition and agreements, utility realignment, excavation, shoring and backfill, footing construction, hazardous material handling, dewatering, erosion control, access restrictions, ground improvement, and owner and neighbor disruption.
key_points: Lineal cost usually exceeds conventional piling, especially driven piles (costs in Chapter 10)
Unlikely to compete on an open site with soft, clean, uniform soils and unrestricted access
Can be most cost-effective for delicate underpinning of a bridge pier in a busy old industrial or residential area
Compare total project cost, e.g., $/kN of axial capacity, not just the unit piling cost
Include right-of-way, utilities, excavation/shoring/backfill, footings, hazardous material, dewatering, erosion control, access, ground improvement, disruption
sections.applicability: Cost comparison of micropiles with conventional piles and the project costs to include.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Micropile structural support applications include foundations for new structures, underpinning of existing structures, scour protection and seismic retrofitting, many on transportation projects; case histories follow.
sections.body: (p. 3-7) Micropile applications for structural support include foundations for new structures, underpinning of existing structures, scour protection and seismic retrofitting of existing structures. Many have been used for transportation projects, and case histories of these applications are given in this section.
key_points: Structural support: new foundations, underpinning, scour protection, seismic retrofit
Case histories from transportation projects follow
sections.applicability: Scope of the structural support case histories.

sections.title: New Foundations
sections.summary: Micropiles suit new bridges needing deep foundations or in difficult ground (cobbles, boulders). I-78 over the Delaware River: Pier E-6 on karstic bedrock, micropiles chosen over drilled shafts for cost and speed after design-phase load tests (Bruce, 1988b). Mahoning Creek, PA: micropiles drilled through stone footings into sandstone, cheapest of three alternatives (Figure 3-4). Brooklyn-Queens Expressway: the only option under low headroom and vibration limits, casing left full length, traffic maintained. Typical uses, Figure 3-5.
sections.body: (pp. 3-7 to 3-9) Micropiles are applicable in new bridge construction where deep foundation alternatives are required or in difficult ground (cobble/boulder obstructions) where conventional piles or drilled shafts are very difficult and/or expensive. For the I-78 dual highway bridge over the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey (Bruce, 1988b), all original piers were on driven piles or spread footings on rock except Pier E-6, where bedrock was deeper than anticipated and karstic; micropiles and drilled shafts were proposed, and micropiles were chosen for lower cost and faster installation in deep karst, after load testing during design (micropiles being fairly new in 1988) showed them feasible. Replacement of a two-span bridge over Mahoning Creek, Armstrong County, Pennsylvania (Pearlman and Wolosick, 1992) needed support for new abutments (Figure 3-4); the original stone abutment foundations, built in cofferdams, sat on erodible soils over competent sandstone; of anchored caisson walls, ground anchors and micropiles, micropiles were least expensive and could be drilled through the existing stone footings into the sandstone. Micropiles allow new bridge foundations under overhead restrictions while maintaining traffic: in the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway deck replacement, Brooklyn, New York (Bruce and Gemme, 1992), micropiles were the only alternative for the new center lane viaduct and ramps because of low headroom and stringent vibration limits; casing was left full length because of the low headroom, traffic flowed during construction, and variable fluvioglacial deposits did not slow installation. Other structural support uses include buildings, earth retaining structures and soundwalls; Figure 3-5 shows typical arrangements for transportation structures.
key_points: Used for new bridges needing deep foundations or in difficult ground (cobble/boulder obstructions)
I-78 Delaware River, Pier E-6: karstic bedrock; micropiles chosen over drilled shafts for cost and speed after design-phase load tests (Bruce, 1988b)
Mahoning Creek, PA: micropiles through existing stone footings into sandstone; least expensive alternative (Pearlman and Wolosick, 1992)
Brooklyn-Queens Expressway: only alternative under low headroom and vibration limits; casing left full length; traffic maintained (Bruce and Gemme, 1992)
Other uses: buildings, earth retaining structures, soundwalls (Figure 3-5)

Figure 3-5: Micropiles for Foundation Support of Transportation Applications (a) bridge foundation support, (b) support for soft ground tunneling beneath existing structures, (c) support for cast-in-place reinforced concrete retaining walls, (d) support for highway soundwalls (p. 3-10)
sections.applicability: Micropiles for new bridge foundations in difficult ground or under overhead restrictions, with case histories.

sections.title: Underpinning of Existing Foundations
sections.summary: Micropiles were developed for underpinning: arresting movement, upgrading capacity, repairing foundations, scour protection, raising settled foundations, transferring load deeper. They can be installed through and bonded within existing structures without new caps. Cases: West Emerson Street Viaduct, Seattle (Figure 3-6); Pocomoke River Bridge, scoured timber piles, preloaded micropiles (Bruce et al., 1990; Figure 3-7); Exton Square Mall, karstic dolomite, column loads up to 4,450 kN (1,000 kips) (Cadden et al., 2001).
sections.body: (pp. 3-9 to 3-12) Micropiles were originally developed for underpinning existing structures, which may be done to arrest and prevent structural movement, upgrade load-bearing capacity, repair or replace deteriorating or inadequate foundations, provide scour protection for erosion-sensitive foundations, raise previously settled foundations, and transfer loads to deeper strata. Micropiles can be installed through and bonded within existing structures, connecting directly to competent underlying strata without new pile caps while reinforcing the structure internally, and construction can proceed without reducing the existing foundation capacity. The West Emerson Street Viaduct in Seattle, Washington (Figure 3-6) needed added support, for tension and compression, at existing bents with tight access and low headroom; micropiles were chosen over low headroom caissons on five bents for their considerably lower cost. Structural movements can come from compressible ground beneath the foundation, dewatering, groundwater fluctuations, foundation deterioration, and adjacent deep excavation and tunneling; micropiles installed to deeper, more competent strata mitigate them. Increased capacity may be needed for added vertical, lateral or vibratory loads from expansion, larger loads or vibrating machinery. The 75-year-old Pocomoke River Bridge in Maryland was rehabilitated when river scour compromised the original wooden piles of the piers (Bruce et al., 1990); the new system, built mid-river, had to be preloaded before connection to prevent further settlement, and micropiles were selected over caissons and installed through the existing foundation (Figure 3-7). Expansion of the Exton Square Mall, Chester County, Pennsylvania (Cadden et al., 2001), on dolomitic limestone classed by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources as hazardous rock (solutioning, sinkholes), needed deep foundations for column loads up to 4,450 kN (1,000 kips); micropiles were chosen over drilled shafts and driven piles for tight access, low headroom, logistics (work while stores were open, interior work at night), irregular rock mass quality and high working loads, and driven piles would likely have been damaged.
key_points: Purposes: arrest movement, upgrade capacity, repair foundations, scour protection, raise settled foundations, transfer load deeper
Installed through and bonded within existing structures, without new pile caps, without reducing existing capacity
West Emerson Street Viaduct, Seattle: tension and compression support at five bents; cheaper than low headroom caissons (Figure 3-6)
Pocomoke River Bridge, MD: scour-damaged timber piles; micropiles preloaded before connection, installed through the existing foundation (Bruce et al., 1990)
Exton Square Mall, PA: karstic dolomitic limestone, column loads up to 4,450 kN (1,000 kips); driven piles would likely be damaged (Cadden et al., 2001)

Figure 3-7: Underpinning Arrangement for Pocomoke River Bridge, Maryland (after Bruce et al., 1990; caption prints 'Underpining') (p. 3-12)

sections.title: Seismic Retrofit
sections.summary: Micropiles are increasingly used for seismic retrofit, especially in California; their near-equal tension and compression capacities optimize added support (Bruce and Chu, 1995). They suit retrofits with limits on footing enlargement, vibration and noise, low headroom, difficult access, high tension and compression demand, difficult drilling or driving, or hazardous soils. Cases: I-110 North Connector, Los Angeles (Pearlman et al., 1993; Figure 3-8); Route 57 near Cairo, Illinois, 240 micropiles under the deck (New Madrid zone).
sections.body: (pp. 3-12 to 3-14) Micropiles are increasingly used for seismic retrofitting of existing highway structures, especially in California; they exhibit near-equal tension and compression capacities, optimizing the added foundation support elements (Bruce and Chu, 1995). They may be economically feasible for bridge foundation retrofits with one or more of: restrictions on footing enlargement; vibration and noise restrictions; low headroom; difficult access; high axial demands in both tension and compression; difficult drilling or driving conditions; and hazardous soil sites. In Caltrans' earthquake retrofit at I-110 in Los Angeles (Pearlman et al., 1993) micropiles were used at the north connector over-crossing (Figure 3-8); drilled shafts were first chosen, but buried concrete obstructions, water-bearing flowing sand layers, low overhead and limited right-of-way prohibited them, and micropiles, designed for tension and compression and connected to the existing structure, were chosen for lower cost and access. Micropiles upgraded existing foundations of a highway bridge on Route 57 near Cairo, Illinois, where seismicity is controlled by the New Madrid Seismic Source Zone, for lateral and vertical design earthquake forces; about 7.5 m (25 ft) of silty clay overlies sands, the existing foundations are short vertical and batter timber piles in the sands, and 240 micropiles were installed under the deck in low headroom, ten just outside each foundation, with reinforcing steel doweled into the existing footing and a new cap poured. Micropiles have also been used for earthquake retrofit of major bridges in the San Francisco Bay area and New York City.
key_points: Increasingly used for seismic retrofit, especially in California; near-equal tension and compression capacities (Bruce and Chu, 1995)
Feasible where footing enlargement is restricted, vibration/noise limited, low headroom, difficult access, high tension and compression demand, difficult drilling, hazardous soils
I-110 North Connector, Los Angeles: drilled shafts prevented by obstructions, flowing sands, low overhead, right-of-way; micropiles in tension and compression (Pearlman et al., 1993)
Route 57 near Cairo, IL (New Madrid zone): 240 micropiles under the deck, ten around each foundation, doweled into a new cap
Also used for retrofit of major bridges in the San Francisco Bay area and New York City
figures: Figure 3-8: Seismic Retrofit of I-110, North Connector, Los Angeles, California (p. 3-13)
sections.applicability: Micropiles for seismic retrofit of bridge foundations, with case histories.

sections.title: In-Situ Reinforcement
sections.summary: Micropiles stabilize slopes in two ways: reticulated networks forming a reinforced-soil gravity wall (CASE 2; Lizzi, 1982), or groups of inclined micropiles tying the moving zone to the stable zone and resisting shear on the failure surface (Pearlman and Wolosick, 1992; Palmerton, 1984; Figure 3-9). In rocky, stiff or dense ground individual shear capacity governs (CASE 1); in loose ground the composite acts as a gravity wall (CASE 2). Cases: SR 4023, PA (about $1 million saved); SH 82 Aspen shoring; Portland Wall 600; Forest Highway 7.
sections.body: (pp. 3-14 to 3-19) Micropiles are used in two different ways to stabilize slopes. Lizzi (1982) suggests reticulated network systems (CASE 2), creating a stable, reinforced-soil 'gravity-retaining wall' in which the reinforced soil mass supplies the essential resisting force and the micropiles supply additional resistance to the tensile and shear forces acting on the 'wall'. Alternately, Pearlman and Wolosick (1992) and Palmerton (1984) suggest groups of individual inclined micropiles connecting the moving zone (above the failure surface) to the stable zone (below it), reinforcing against the shearing forces along the failure surface; typical inclined group configurations for slope stabilization and earth retention are shown in Figure 3-9. For rocky, stiff or dense materials the shear resistance of the micropiles across the failure surface (individual capacity) is critical (CASE 1); for loose materials the micropiles and soil are mutually reinforcing, creating a gravity wall, and individual capacities are less significant (CASE 2). State Road 4023, Armstrong County, Pennsylvania (Bruce, 1988a): a 75-m (250-ft) section of road and upslope railroad tracks was damaged by slope movement toward a river; rock anchors and tangent drilled shafts into rock were proposed, but alternative bidding allowed inclined micropile groups, accepted for savings of about $1 million against the lowest anchored drilled shaft bid; the wall had four rows of micropiles across the failure plane into competent rock (Figure 3-10). State Highway 82 near Aspen, Colorado (Macklin et al., 2004): micropiles gave temporary excavation support in loose to very dense silty to gravelly sand with cobbles and boulders (debris flow, sheet wash, colluvium) over dense alluvial sandy gravel; chosen over soil nails and tiebacks to improve schedule and phasing, the shoring was a hybrid of soldier beam and lagging and soil nailing (Figure 3-11) and let the contractor transition access road grades for each phase of bridge construction. Portland Westside Light-Rail, Oregon (Ueblacker, 1996): Wall 600, about 183 m (600 ft) long with cuts of 4 to 9.5 m (13 to 30 ft), replaced a counterfort wall on driven piles as a contractor-proposed value engineering alternate that fit the right-of-way, with vertical and inclined micropiles (Figure 3-12), temporary shotcrete and a permanent architectural cast-in-place facing. Forest Highway 7, Mendocino National Forest, California (Palmerton, 1984), an early reticulated slope stabilization and one of two reticulated micropile structures in the U.S. at the time, chosen as a demonstration although cantilever or anchored walls could have worked: a 94-m (305-ft) section of road across a rain-triggered landslide (Figures 3-13, 3-14). Feasibility is discussed further in Chapter 5 (structural support) and Chapter 6 (slope stabilization).
key_points: Two concepts: reticulated network forming a reinforced-soil gravity wall (CASE 2; Lizzi, 1982), or inclined micropile groups tying moving to stable zone (Pearlman and Wolosick, 1992; Palmerton, 1984)
Rocky, stiff or dense ground: individual micropile shear capacity across the failure surface is critical (CASE 1)
Loose ground: micropiles and soil mutually reinforce as a gravity wall; individual capacity less significant (CASE 2)
SR 4023, PA: four rows of inclined micropiles into rock; about $1 million saved against an anchored drilled shaft wall (Bruce, 1988a)
SH 82 near Aspen, CO: temporary micropile shoring, a hybrid of soldier beam and lagging and soil nailing (Macklin et al., 2004)
Portland Wall 600: about 183 m long, 4-9.5 m cuts; value engineering alternate within the right-of-way (Ueblacker, 1996)
Forest Highway 7, CA: 94-m reticulated micropile slope stabilization, a demonstration project (Palmerton, 1984)
